title: Acting on design feedback
idea: Iterating on feedback means turning each comment into a check that fails, changing the design until it passes, and telling the reviewer what changed.
points: Sort comments first: bugs, then missing requirements, then style.
Write a check that reproduces the comment before you change code.
Change the smallest class that owns the rule, here `ConflictPolicy`.
Rerun every check, then reply with what changed and why.

edges.caption: A reviewer says a booking from 11 to 12 is refused after one ending at 11.
It breaks a requirement, so it is a bug: it goes first.
A check proves the bug; the overlap rule lives in one class, so only that class changes.
Run every check, not only the new one, so the fix breaks nothing else.
Tell the reviewer what changed and which check now guards it.

edges.label: still failing
edges.caption: If a check still fails, change again; the loop ends only when all pass.

code.title: Reproduce, then fix
code.caption: Suppose your first policy used `<=`. The reviewer's comment becomes a check; `<` lets touching slots pass.

walk.text: Three bookings: one held 10 to 11, one right after it, one inside it.
The old policy uses `<=`, so a slot ending at 11 blocks one starting at 11.
The fix uses `<`. A slot covers its start but not its end, so 11 is free.
The same two checks run against both versions: the old one fails back-to-back, the new one passes both.
A tiny hand-written runner; teams use JUnit 5 for this.

pitfalls: Do not change code before a check reproduces the comment.
Avoid fixing several comments in one change; one comment, one change, one reply.
takeaway: Reproduce the comment as a check, fix the owner, rerun everything, reply.

starters: What if I disagree with a reviewer's comment?
How do I prioritise feedback when there is too much to fix?
Why are time slots treated as half-open intervals?
